q: Why is C called a compiled language?
a: The whole source is translated to machine code before it runs, so errors surface at compile time and execution is fast.
explain: The whole source is translated to machine code before it runs, so errors surface at compile time and execution is fast.

q: What does #include <stdio.h> do?
a: It pastes the declarations of standard I/O functions (printf, scanf, FILE) so the compiler knows their signatures.
explain: It pastes the declarations of standard I/O functions (printf, scanf, FILE) so the compiler knows their signatures.

q: Difference between declaration and definition?
a: Declaration announces a type/signature; definition allocates storage or provides the body. A variable can be declared many times, defined once.
explain: Declaration announces a type/signature; definition allocates storage or provides the body. A variable can be declared many times, defined once.

q: What is the entry point of a C program?
a: main(). Execution starts there; its return value becomes the process exit status.
explain: main(). Execution starts there; its return value becomes the process exit status.

q: Why does sizeof(int) differ across platforms?
a: The C standard only guarantees minimum ranges, not exact widths. Use sizeof and <stdint.h> for portability.
explain: The C standard only guarantees minimum ranges, not exact widths. Use sizeof and <stdint.h> for portability.

q: What is integer overflow?
a: A result outside the type's range. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned wraps modulo 2^N and is defined.
explain: A result outside the type's range. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned wraps modulo 2^N and is defined.

a: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1/0.2 exactly, so the sum is slightly off. Compare with an epsilon.
explain: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1/0.2 exactly, so the sum is slightly off. Compare with an epsilon.

q: Why does scanf need & before an int?
a: scanf must write into the variable, so it needs the address. Arrays already decay to an address, so no & for %s.
explain: scanf must write into the variable, so it needs the address. Arrays already decay to an address, so no & for %s.

q: Why is fgets safer than scanf("%s")?
a: fgets takes a buffer size and cannot overflow; bare %s has no bound and can write past the array.
explain: fgets takes a buffer size and cannot overflow; bare %s has no bound and can write past the array.

q: What is short-circuit evaluation?
a: && and || stop evaluating once the result is known, which lets you guard a dereference or a division.
explain: && and || stop evaluating once the result is known, which lets you guard a dereference or a division.

q: Difference between ++i and i++?
a: Prefix increments then yields the new value; postfix yields the old value then increments.
explain: Prefix increments then yields the new value; postfix yields the old value then increments.

q: Why prefer braces around if bodies?
a: Without braces a second statement silently falls outside the condition, and the dangling else binds to the nearest if.
explain: Without braces a second statement silently falls outside the condition, and the dangling else binds to the nearest if.

q: When is switch better than if-else?
a: For discrete integral values (menu, state). Ranges and complex conditions need if-else.
explain: For discrete integral values (menu, state). Ranges and complex conditions need if-else.

q: Difference between while and do-while?
a: while tests before the body (may run zero times); do-while tests after (runs at least once).
explain: while tests before the body (may run zero times); do-while tests after (runs at least once).

q: How do you avoid an infinite loop?
a: Guarantee progress inside the body (update the loop variable) and make the exit condition reachable.
explain: Guarantee progress inside the body (update the loop variable) and make the exit condition reachable.

q: Why pass a struct by pointer?
a: To avoid copying and to let the callee modify the original. Use const pointer when only reading.
explain: To avoid copying and to let the callee modify the original. Use const pointer when only reading.

q: What is a function prototype for?
a: It tells the compiler the signature before the call, enabling type checking and preventing implicit declarations.
explain: It tells the compiler the signature before the call, enabling type checking and preventing implicit declarations.

q: Can C return multiple values?
a: Not directly. Return a struct or use pointer out-parameters.
explain: Not directly. Return a struct or use pointer out-parameters.

q: When does recursion overflow the stack?
a: When depth grows without a reachable base case, or the depth exceeds the thread's stack (large n).
explain: When depth grows without a reachable base case, or the depth exceeds the thread's stack (large n).

q: Why is naive Fibonacci slow?
a: It recomputes the same subproblems, giving O(2^n). Memoization or iteration reduces it to O(n).
explain: It recomputes the same subproblems, giving O(2^n). Memoization or iteration reduces it to O(n).

q: Why doesn't sizeof give the array size inside a function?
a: The array parameter decays to a pointer, so sizeof returns the pointer's size. Pass the length separately.
explain: The array parameter decays to a pointer, so sizeof returns the pointer's size. Pass the length separately.

q: How is a 2D array laid out?
a: Row-major: all columns of row 0, then row 1. Address = base + (i*cols + j)*element_size.
explain: Row-major: all columns of row 0, then row 1. Address = base + (i*cols + j)*element_size.

q: Why must a string have a null terminator?
a: Library functions (strlen, %s) stop at '�'; without it they read past the buffer.
explain: Library functions (strlen, %s) stop at '�'; without it they read past the buffer.

q: Why is strncpy easy to misuse?
a: It does not null-terminate when the source is too long, and pads with zeros when shorter. Set the terminator yourself or use snprintf.
explain: It does not null-terminate when the source is too long, and pads with zeros when shorter. Set the terminator yourself or use snprintf.

q: What does strcmp return?
a: 0 if equal, negative if the first is lexicographically smaller, positive if greater.
explain: 0 if equal, negative if the first is lexicographically smaller, positive if greater.

q: What is a dangling pointer?
a: A pointer to memory that was freed or went out of scope. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.
explain: A pointer to memory that was freed or went out of scope. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.

q: What does pointer arithmetic p+1 mean?
a: It advances by one element (sizeof *p bytes), not one byte.
explain: It advances by one element (sizeof *p bytes), not one byte.

q: Difference between const int *p and int *const p?
a: The first makes the pointee read-only; the second makes the pointer itself read-only.
explain: The first makes the pointee read-only; the second makes the pointer itself read-only.

q: What is a void pointer used for?
a: A generic address holder (malloc, callbacks). It cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic without a cast.
explain: A generic address holder (malloc, callbacks). It cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic without a cast.

q: Why does sizeof(struct) exceed the sum of members?
a: Padding and alignment: the compiler inserts gaps so each member sits at a proper boundary.
explain: Padding and alignment: the compiler inserts gaps so each member sits at a proper boundary.

q: Union vs struct?
a: A struct stores every member separately; a union shares one storage area, so only one member is valid at a time.
explain: A struct stores every member separately; a union shares one storage area, so only one member is valid at a time.

q: Why check the return value of fopen?
a: It returns NULL on failure (missing file, permissions), and using NULL crashes.
explain: It returns NULL on failure (missing file, permissions), and using NULL crashes.

q: Difference between "w" and "a"?
a: "w" truncates or creates; "a" appends without destroying existing content.
explain: "w" truncates or creates; "a" appends without destroying existing content.

q: Difference between malloc and calloc?
a: malloc returns uninitialized bytes; calloc zeroes them and takes count and size.
explain: malloc returns uninitialized bytes; calloc zeroes them and takes count and size.

q: What happens if realloc fails?
a: It returns NULL and the original block stays valid — assign to a temporary or you leak it.
explain: It returns NULL and the original block stays valid — assign to a temporary or you leak it.

q: What is a double free?
a: Calling free twice on the same pointer. It corrupts the allocator and is undefined behaviour.
explain: Calling free twice on the same pointer. It corrupts the allocator and is undefined behaviour.

q: How do you detect memory leaks?
a: AddressSanitizer or Valgrind in development, heap profilers in production, plus explicit ownership rules.
explain: AddressSanitizer or Valgrind in development, heap profilers in production, plus explicit ownership rules.

q: Where do local variables live?
a: On the stack, with automatic lifetime tied to the block. Large or runtime-sized data belongs on the heap.
explain: On the stack, with automatic lifetime tied to the block. Large or runtime-sized data belongs on the heap.

q: What is a function pointer good for?
a: Runtime dispatch and callbacks — qsort comparators, menu tables, event handlers.
explain: Runtime dispatch and callbacks — qsort comparators, menu tables, event handlers.

q: Why can two pointers not be meaningfully compared across arrays?
a: Only pointers into the same array object (plus one past the end) have defined ordering; anything else is unspecified.
explain: Only pointers into the same array object (plus one past the end) have defined ordering; anything else is unspecified.

q: Why are macros dangerous?
a: Text substitution ignores scope and types, can double-evaluate arguments, and produces confusing errors. Prefer inline functions.
explain: Text substitution ignores scope and types, can double-evaluate arguments, and produces confusing errors. Prefer inline functions.

q: What is a header guard?
a: #ifndef/#define/#endif around a header so multiple includes do not redefine its contents.
explain: #ifndef/#define/#endif around a header so multiple includes do not redefine its contents.

q: How do you build a multi-file project?
a: Compile each .c to .o, then link: gcc main.c util.c -o app. Keep declarations in headers.
explain: Compile each .c to .o, then link: gcc main.c util.c -o app. Keep declarations in headers.

q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
a: Each comparison halves the remaining range, so the number of steps is logarithmic.
explain: Each comparison halves the remaining range, so the number of steps is logarithmic.

q: Which sorts are stable?
a: Merge sort, insertion sort, bubble sort (with strict comparison). Quick sort and selection sort are not stable by default.
explain: Merge sort, insertion sort, bubble sort (with strict comparison). Quick sort and selection sort are not stable by default.

q: When does quick sort degrade to O(n^2)?
a: When partitions are extremely unbalanced, e.g. always picking the first element of a sorted array as pivot.
explain: When partitions are extremely unbalanced, e.g. always picking the first element of a sorted array as pivot.

q: What is two-pointer technique?
a: Walking two indices from ends or in the same direction to solve pair/window problems in O(n) on sorted or monotonic data.
explain: Walking two indices from ends or in the same direction to solve pair/window problems in O(n) on sorted or monotonic data.

q: Array vs linked list?
a: Array gives O(1) indexing but O(n) insert/delete; a linked list gives O(1) insert/delete at a known node but O(n) access.
explain: Array gives O(1) indexing but O(n) insert/delete; a linked list gives O(1) insert/delete at a known node but O(n) access.

q: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
a: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one node, fast two; they meet if a cycle exists.
explain: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one node, fast two; they meet if a cycle exists.

q: Stack vs queue?
a: Stack is LIFO (push/pop at top); queue is FIFO (enqueue at rear, dequeue at front).
explain: Stack is LIFO (push/pop at top); queue is FIFO (enqueue at rear, dequeue at front).

q: Why is a hash table average O(1)?
a: The hash function maps a key directly to a bucket; with a low load factor collisions are rare.
explain: The hash function maps a key directly to a bucket; with a low load factor collisions are rare.

q: What is the worst case for a BST?
a: A skewed tree behaves like a linked list, so search becomes O(n). Balanced trees guarantee O(log n).
explain: A skewed tree behaves like a linked list, so search becomes O(n). Balanced trees guarantee O(log n).

q: What does a segmentation fault mean?
a: The process accessed memory it does not own — NULL dereference, freed memory, or out-of-bounds access.
explain: The process accessed memory it does not own — NULL dereference, freed memory, or out-of-bounds access.

q: How does AddressSanitizer help?
a: It instruments memory accesses and reports the exact line for overflow, use-after-free, double free and leaks.
explain: It instruments memory accesses and reports the exact line for overflow, use-after-free, double free and leaks.

q: What is undefined behaviour?
a: Code the standard places no requirements on — signed overflow, out-of-bounds, uninitialized reads. The compiler may do anything.
explain: Code the standard places no requirements on — signed overflow, out-of-bounds, uninitialized reads. The compiler may do anything.

q: What does -Wall -Wextra do?
a: Enables a large set of useful compiler warnings; -Werror turns them into errors so they cannot be ignored.
explain: Enables a large set of useful compiler warnings; -Werror turns them into errors so they cannot be ignored.

q: What is the difference between -c and linking?
a: -c compiles and assembles to an object file; linking resolves symbols and combines objects and libraries into an executable.
explain: -c compiles and assembles to an object file; linking resolves symbols and combines objects and libraries into an executable.

q: Why is `a[i]` the same as `*(a+i)`?
a: Array subscripting is defined as pointer arithmetic on the decayed pointer; both forms are equivalent expressions.
explain: Array subscripting is defined as pointer arithmetic on the decayed pointer; both forms are equivalent expressions.

q: Is `char *s = "hi"; s[0]='H';` legal?
a: No. A string literal is read-only; modifying it is undefined behaviour. Use `char s[] = "hi";`.
explain: No. A string literal is read-only; modifying it is undefined behaviour. Use `char s[] = "hi";`.
